pages.cardBlurb: The two numbers on every rated rain jacket — water penetration and breathability — and why the second one decides comfort.
pages.metaTitle: EN 343 Explained: Waterproof Jacket Ratings | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: EN 343's two class numbers decoded — water penetration (1–4) and breathability (1–4) — why a 4:1 jacket soaks you from inside, and how to pick classes by exposure.
pages.lede: "Waterproof" on a work jacket is a certified claim with two numbers behind it: how hard the fabric resists rain getting in, and how well it lets sweat get out. Most buying mistakes come from reading only the first one.

blocks.h2: Keeping rain out is half the job
blocks.html:
EN 343 rates protective clothing against rain with two classes, shown together on the garment pictogram:

  • X — resistance to water penetration (class 1–4): how much water pressure the fabric and seams withstand before leaking. Class 4, added in the current revision, is tested after pre-treatment that simulates wear.
  • Y — water vapour resistance (class 1–4): breathability. Higher class = sweat vapour escapes more easily.

The second number is where comfort lives. A worker generating heat inside a non-breathable shell gets wet from their own sweat as surely as from rain — colder, clammier and slower to dry. That's the 4:1 trap: maximum penetration resistance, minimum breathability, miserable by mid-morning if the work is physical.

blocks.lead: Pick both numbers to the work, not just the rain.

blocks.h2: EN 343 performance is maintained, not just bought
blocks.html:
The certified performance assumes the garment's DWR coating is alive and its seams intact. When rain stops beading and the face fabric wets out, breathability collapses and the jacket "leaks" without leaking — the fix is cleaning and reproofing, covered step-by-step in reproofing waterproofs.

On hi-vis waterproofs, remember the garment is certified twice over — the rain rating and EN ISO 20471 visibility — and each wash counts against the hi-vis wash limit. Buy once, maintain deliberately.

faq.q: What do the EN 343 numbers mean?
faq.a: Two classes, each 1–4: the first is resistance to water penetration (how hard rain is kept out), the second is water vapour resistance (breathability — how easily sweat escapes). Higher is better in both; the current revision added class 4 penetration, tested after simulated wear.

faq.q: Is a class 4 EN 343 jacket the best?
faq.a: Only if the breathability class is healthy too. A 4:1 garment keeps rain out and sweat in — fine for static roles, miserable for physical work. For high-output outdoor trades, aim for 3 or 4 in both positions.

faq.q: Why does my EN 343 jacket feel like it leaks?
faq.a: Usually it's wetting out, not leaking: the DWR coating has worn off, the face fabric soaks up water, and breathability collapses — so sweat condenses inside. Washing the jacket clean and applying a wash-in reproofer restores it; genuine leaks track to seams or damage.

faq.q: Does EN 343 mean the jacket is warm?
faq.a: No — EN 343 covers rain only. Cold protection is a separate standard (EN 342 for below −5 °C environments), which is why winter site jackets are often certified to both, or worn as a shell over insulating layers.

pages.cardBlurb: The standard behind cold-store suits — what the insulation value means, and why sweat is the real enemy at minus twenty.
pages.h1: EN 342: dressing for below minus five.
pages.metaDesc: What EN 342 certifies on cold-store suits and freezer kit — the insulation value, air permeability classes, how wear-time works at −25 °C, and why sweat management decides comfort.
pages.lede: EN 342 is the standard nobody meets until they take a cold-store job — then it's the number on the suit that decides whether a −25 °C shift is routine or miserable. Here's what it certifies, and the sweat-management logic the label can't teach.

heroMeta.l: The real enemy in the cold

blocks.h2: Insulation you can compare between garments
blocks.html:
EN 342 covers clothing — usually suits, or jacket-and-trouser ensembles — for environments below −5 °C: cold stores, blast freezers, winter outdoor work in genuinely cold conditions. The label carries:

  • The insulation value (Icler) — measured thermal insulation of the garment as worn, moving. Higher = warmer, and because it's a standard test, two suits' values compare directly.
  • Air permeability class (1–3) — how windproof the shell is. Class 3 is the tightest; it matters wherever air moves, which includes the fan wall of a blast freezer.
  • Optional water penetration class — for cold that comes with wet.

Manufacturers publish tables translating insulation values into safe wear times by temperature and activity level — the practical planning tool for freezer rotations.

blocks.lead: Three standards cover "cold" — buy the one that matches the thermometer.

blocks.h2: At minus twenty, sweat beats cold as the hazard
blocks.html:
The counterintuitive rule of freezer work: over-dressing is as dangerous as under-dressing. Work hard in too much insulation, sweat into the layers, and the moisture kills the suit's warmth from inside — the second half of the shift is spent cold in wet kit. That's why EN 342 suits are sized to fit over a wicking base layer, not a pile of jumpers, and why door-transition roles (chamber to ambient and back) need layers they can vent.

The extremities aren't in the suit's rating: CI-marked insulated footwear (the boot codes), lined gloves and covered ears complete the system. The operational side — rotations, zones, who buys what — is in the warehouse sector guide.

items.l: Shared suits end up sweat-damp and unworn — name them like boots
A wicking base under the suit outperforms a jumper under it, every time
Evaporator fans add wind-chill the thermometer hides — air permeability class 3 near fan walls

faq.q: What is EN 342 on a cold store suit?
faq.a: The European standard for protective clothing against cold below −5 °C. The label's insulation value (measured as worn, moving) lets you compare garments directly, alongside an air-permeability (windproofing) class and an optional water-penetration class.

faq.q: What's the difference between EN 342 and EN 14058?
faq.a: Temperature scope: EN 342 covers genuinely cold environments below −5 °C — freezer and cold-store territory; EN 14058 covers cool environments above that, where lined bodywarmers and winter mid-layers do the job. Blast-freezer work is always EN 342 kit.

faq.q: Why do I still get cold in a rated freezer suit?
faq.a: Most often it's sweat: over-layering under the suit or over-working in it dampens the insulation, which then loses its warmth. Wear a wicking base layer, size the suit as designed, and vent during warm-side tasks. Wind-chill from evaporator fans is the other hidden factor.

faq.q: How long can you work at −25 °C?
faq.a: It depends on the garment's insulation value and your activity level — manufacturers publish wear-time tables matching insulation values to temperatures and work rates, and employers build rotation schedules from them. The suit's rating is the input, not the answer.
